evidence: Marked option 3 (Uplink RAN Configuration Transfer) is defensible but so is option 2 (Downlink RAN Configuration Transfer). TS 38.413 V17.10.0 has no procedure named for inter-system load balancing. The inter-system load reporting is carried in the Inter-system SON Configuration Transfer IE (9.3.3.33), which the CR history labels 'NGAP Inter-System Load Balancing corrections' (RP-221141). The Inter-system Resource Status Request/Report/Reply IEs (9.3.3.59-61) ride inside that IE. The IE can be sent NG-RAN->E-UTRAN in UPLINK RAN CONFIGURATION TRANSFER (9.2.7.1, clause 8.8.1) and E-UTRAN->NG-RAN in DOWNLINK RAN CONFIGURATION TRANSFER (9.2.7.2, clause 8.8.2). Clause 8.8.2 also says the NG-RAN handles the Inter-system SON Information Request/Reply and Report there. Both options 2 and 3 are therefore plausible, and the question does not specify direction, so it cannot be called uniquely right. Options 1 and 4 (eNB/MME Configuration Transfer) are E-UTRAN-side and are not NGAP procedures for this purpose. I also did not find an explicit statement that any single one is 'the' inter-system load balancing procedure.

The marked option 5 (Europe) does not match a 30 dBm limit for 5725-5850 MHz. The European generic SRD limit for 5725-5875 MHz is 25 mW (about 14 dBm) EIRP, and the Europe-specific 400 mW tier with mitigation is about 26 dBm, not 30 dBm. The 30 dBm figure is the US limit: FCC 47 CFR 15.407 (formerly 15.247) allows 1 W (30 dBm) maximum conducted output power across 5725-5850 MHz. Option 2 (United States) is therefore the correct answer. Caveat: Canada (ISED RSS-247) may mirror the FCC 1 W conducted limit, so option 3 is not fully excluded, but the marked answer of Europe is clearly wrong. I did not verify Canada's RSS-247 text directly.

evidence: IEEE C95.1 does not rank RF hazards by harm, so 'most harmful' is not defined by the standard. The standard's protections cover established adverse effects: electrostimulation (3 kHz to 5 MHz), heating (localized and whole-body, 100 kHz to 300 GHz), and RF shocks and burns (contact-current and contact-voltage limits, Section 4.5).
